To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the transient amplification of waves in disks is a robust and convergent phenomenon, (2) vortices in Keplerian disks are unstable to bending and are not a viable route to hydrodynamic turbulence, and (3) the residual transport in three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations of vortices is dominated by slowly decaying large-scale vorticity.

(a) our numerical methods are accurate and converge at second order; (b) in three dimensions, vortices decay more rapidly than in two dimensions, due to bending modes, and the residual transport is at least an order of magnitude smaller; (c) in three dimensions there is no evidence for sustained hydrodynamical turbulence and transport; (d) at late times, large-scale vorticities dominate the residual transport, with additional contributions from inertial waves possible.

three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations of vortices do not support the idea that hydrodynamic turbulence is a viable mechanism for angular momentum transport in disks, and that large-scale vorticities are a viable mechanism for transport.

the role of hydrodynamic turbulence and the resulting transport is not as important as it was thought to be, and that the role of large-scale vorticity and the resulting transport should be further investigated in the context of astrophysical disks.
